title: The Hardy–Ramanujan Partition Asymptotic
subject: Number Theory
statement: The partition function p(n), counting unordered sums of positive integers, satisfies p(n) asymptotic to exp(pi sqrt(2n/3))/(4n sqrt(3)).
short: The number of partitions grows exponentially in the square root of n.
long: The number of partitions grows exponentially in the square root of n. Rademacher later gave an exact convergent series for p(n) using the circle method.
proof: The generating function is the reciprocal of the Euler product prod(1−q^k), and the circle method near the roots of unity gives the main term from the dominant singularity at q=1.
consequence: It is a founding success of the circle method and links partitions to modular forms.

title: Zermelo–Fraenkel Set Theory with the Axiom of Choice
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: ZFC is the standard axiomatic foundation of mathematics, consisting of the Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms together with the axiom of choice.
short: ZFC is the accepted rulebook for what counts as a set.
long: ZFC is the accepted rulebook for what counts as a set. Key axioms include extensionality, pairing, union, power set, replacement, infinity and regularity, with separation and replacement as axiom schemas.
proof: The axioms are taken as primitive; their consistency relative to weaker systems is studied via inner models and forcing, while Gödel's theorems preclude an absolute finitary consistency proof.
consequence: Almost all mainstream mathematics can be formalised in ZFC.

title: Equivalent Formulations of the Axiom of Choice
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: The axiom of choice is equivalent to Zorn's lemma, the well-ordering theorem, Tychonoff's theorem for compact spaces, and the statement that every surjection has a section.
short: Many apparently different principles are really the same choice axiom in disguise.
long: Many apparently different principles are really the same choice axiom in disguise. The equivalence with Zorn's lemma is the version most often used in algebra.
proof: Each equivalence is proved by deriving one principle from another using the cumulative hierarchy and transfinite recursion; for example Zorn's lemma follows from choice by building a maximal chain.
consequence: The axiom is indispensable for many existence results but has counterintuitive consequences such as Banach–Tarski.

title: Zorn's Lemma for Maximal Elements
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If every chain in a nonempty partially ordered set has an upper bound, then the set has a maximal element.
short: Zorn's lemma produces maximal objects from chain-closed conditions.
long: Zorn's lemma produces maximal objects from chain-closed conditions. It is equivalent to the axiom of choice over ZF.
proof: Assume no maximal element and use choice to define a function selecting a strict upper bound for every element; transfinite recursion then builds a chain with no upper bound, a contradiction.
consequence: It proves existence of bases in vector spaces, maximal ideals and algebraic closures.

title: The Well-Ordering Theorem
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Every set can be well-ordered, meaning it admits a total order in which every nonempty subset has a least element.
short: Choice lets you line up any set, even an uncountable one, in a well-order.
long: Choice lets you line up any set, even an uncountable one, in a well-order. For the reals this well-order cannot be explicitly described in ZFC in any simple way.
proof: Zermelo's proof uses choice to pick an element from each nonempty subset and transfinite recursion to enumerate the set until exhausted.
consequence: It generalises induction to arbitrary sets and underlies cardinal comparison.

title: Cantor's Theorem on the Power Set
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: For every set A the power set of A has strictly larger cardinality than A.
short: There are always more subsets than elements.
long: There are always more subsets than elements. The diagonal argument gives an injection A into P(A) but no surjection.
proof: An injection sends a to {a}; if f:A→P(A) were surjective, the set {a∈A:a not in f(a)} would differ from every f(a), a contradiction.
consequence: It yields an infinite hierarchy of infinite cardinals.

title: The Continuum Hypothesis
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: The continuum hypothesis asserts that there is no cardinal strictly between the cardinality of the natural numbers and that of the reals.
short: Is there any infinity strictly between the countable and the continuum?
long: Is there any infinity strictly between the countable and the continuum? The statement is neither provable nor refutable from ZFC assuming ZFC is consistent.
proof: Cantor posed it and believed it true; the status was settled only by Gödel and Cohen through constructibility and forcing.
consequence: It shows that familiar set-theoretic questions can be undecidable in the standard axioms.

title: The Independence of the Continuum Hypothesis
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Assuming ZFC is consistent, the continuum hypothesis can neither be proved nor disproved from ZFC.
short: The continuum hypothesis can be true in some models of set theory and false in others.
long: The continuum hypothesis can be true in some models of set theory and false in others. Gödel showed CH holds in the constructible universe; Cohen showed models of ZFC where the continuum is larger than aleph-one.
proof: Gödel built the inner model L satisfying the generalized continuum hypothesis; Cohen invented forcing to add many reals while preserving ZFC, producing a model where the continuum exceeds aleph-one.
consequence: It inaugurated the modern study of independence phenomena in set theory.

title: Forcing and Generic Extensions of Models of Set Theory
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Forcing constructs a larger model of set theory by adjoining a generic filter on a partially ordered set of conditions, carefully chosen so that no new contradictions arise.
short: Forcing builds new universes of sets by adding carefully controlled generic objects.
long: Forcing builds new universes of sets by adding carefully controlled generic objects. The forcing relation lets one decide in the ground model which statements the generic extension will satisfy.
proof: Start with a countable transitive model, choose a poset and an M-generic filter, define names for sets, and verify that the interpretation of all names gives a model satisfying ZFC.
consequence: It is the principal method for proving independence results across set theory.

title: The Constructible Universe L
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Gödel's constructible universe L is the class built by transfinitely iterating the operation of taking definable subsets, and it satisfies ZFC together with the generalized continuum hypothesis.
short: L is the smallest inner model containing all ordinals and satisfying ZFC.
long: L is the smallest inner model containing all ordinals and satisfying ZFC. The statement that every set is constructible is the axiom V=L, which implies CH but is not forced by ZFC.
proof: Define L_α recursively using first-order definability over previous levels; verifying the ZFC axioms uses the condensation lemma, and GCH follows from a fine structure argument.
consequence: It provides the canonical inner model for relative consistency proofs.

title: Measurable Cardinals and Large Cardinal Axioms
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A measurable cardinal is an uncountable cardinal κ carrying a nonprincipal κ-complete ultrafilter; such cardinals cannot be proved to exist in ZFC alone.
short: Large cardinals are extra robustness assumptions far beyond ZFC.
long: Large cardinals are extra robustness assumptions far beyond ZFC. Measurable cardinals imply that L is not the whole universe and have strong consequences for projective determinacy.
proof: Scott's theorem shows that if a measurable cardinal exists then V differs from L, since the ultrapower by a measure would otherwise contradict rigidity of L.
consequence: They form a hierarchy measuring the consistency strength of strong set-theoretic statements.

title: Ordinal Arithmetic and Its Noncommutativity
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Ordinal addition, multiplication and exponentiation are defined by transfinite recursion and are generally noncommutative; for example 1+ω=ω but ω+1>ω.
short: For infinite ordinals, the order of operations matters.
long: For infinite ordinals, the order of operations matters. Ordinal arithmetic describes order types rather than sizes, unlike cardinal arithmetic.
proof: Ordinal addition is defined by concatenating well-orders, so appending one point after all naturals gives a different order type from putting it before them.
consequence: It is the algebra of transfinite processes and induction.

title: Transfinite Induction and Recursion
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If a property holds at zero, at successors whenever it holds at the predecessor, and at limit ordinals whenever it holds at all earlier ordinals, then it holds for every ordinal.
short: Induction works on ordinals provided one handles limit stages separately.
long: Induction works on ordinals provided one handles limit stages separately. Transfinite recursion similarly defines functions on all ordinals from their earlier values.
proof: If some ordinal failed the property, the least such ordinal could not be zero, a successor or a limit, a contradiction.
consequence: It underlies constructions such as the cumulative hierarchy and well-ordering proofs.

title: The Burali-Forti Paradox
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: The collection of all ordinals cannot itself be a set, since it would be well-ordered and hence an ordinal larger than every ordinal, including itself.
short: The ordinals are too numerous to form a completed set.
long: The ordinals are too numerous to form a completed set. A similar paradox arises for the collection of all cardinals.
proof: Any set of ordinals has a supremum which is an ordinal greater than all its members; applying this to the alleged set of all ordinals gives a contradiction.
consequence: It motivates the set/class distinction in axiomatic set theory.

title: Russell's Paradox and the Limits of Naive Comprehension
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: The set of all sets that are not members of themselves cannot exist, because it is a member of itself exactly when it is not.
latex: R=\{x:x\notin x\},\quad R\in R\iff R\notin R
short: Unrestricted set formation is logically inconsistent.
long: Unrestricted set formation is logically inconsistent. Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory replaces comprehension by separation, allowing only subsets of an existing set.
proof: Assume R is a set; asking whether R belongs to R gives the contradiction directly from its definition.
consequence: It forced the axiomatisation of set theory and reshaped the foundations of mathematics.

title: The Schröder–Bernstein Theorem
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If there are injections from A into B and from B into A, then there is a bijection between A and B.
short: Mutual embeddability of sets forces equal cardinality.
long: Mutual embeddability of sets forces equal cardinality. The proof does not require the axiom of choice.
proof: Track elements under alternating applications of the two injections; partition each set into chains and cycles and define a bijection by following the injections on one family of chains and their inverses on the rest.
consequence: It defines cardinal comparison without needing a well-ordering of the sets.

title: König's Theorem on Cardinal Sums
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If κ_i < λ_i for every i in an index set, then the sum of the κ_i is strictly less than the product of the λ_i.
short: A product of larger cardinals always outruns a sum of smaller ones.
long: A product of larger cardinals always outruns a sum of smaller ones. The special case with all κ_i finite and λ_i=2 gives Cantor's theorem.
proof: Given a map from the disjoint union into the product, diagonalise by choosing for each index a value of λ_i not used by the corresponding component.
consequence: It gives the consistency of the axiom of choice with ZF and strong inequalities in cardinal arithmetic.

title: The Hartogs Number of a Set
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: For every set A there is a least ordinal that cannot be injected into A, called the Hartogs number of A.
short: Every set has a well-ordered size that it cannot absorb.
long: Every set has a well-ordered size that it cannot absorb. Hartogs numbers exist in ZF without the axiom of choice and give the smallest well-ordered cardinal not dominated by A.
proof: Consider the set of well-orderings of subsets of A and take the supremum of their order types; the next ordinal cannot inject into A.
consequence: It is used to prove that every set can be well-ordered if and only if the axiom of choice holds.

title: Łoś's Theorem and Ultraproducts
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: In an ultraproduct of structures, a first-order sentence holds in the ultraproduct if and only if the set of indices where it holds belongs to the ultrafilter.
short: Ultraproducts transfer first-order truth from components modulo an ultrafilter.
long: Ultraproducts transfer first-order truth from components modulo an ultrafilter. Łoś's theorem is the fundamental theorem of ultraproducts and underlies nonstandard analysis.
proof: Prove by induction on formulas; atomic cases follow from the definition, boolean connectives use ultrafilter closure, and existential quantifiers use a choice function on a set in the ultrafilter.
consequence: It yields compactness, nonstandard models of the reals and transfer principles.

title: Quantifier Elimination in Model Theory
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A theory has quantifier elimination if every formula is equivalent modulo the theory to a formula containing no quantifiers.
short: Quantifier elimination reduces logical complexity to explicit conditions.
long: Quantifier elimination reduces logical complexity to explicit conditions. The theory of algebraically closed fields and the theory of real closed fields both have quantifier elimination in suitable languages.
proof: Eliminate one quantifier at a time by constructing a quantifier-free equivalent using the algebraic or order-theoretic structure, then iterate.
consequence: It yields decidability and geometric descriptions of definable sets.

title: The Tarski–Vaught Test for Elementary Substructures
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A subset A of a structure M is the universe of an elementary substructure if and only if every existential formula with parameters from A that holds in M has a witness in A.
short: Elementary substructures are exactly those that realise every existential demand they can express.
long: Elementary substructures are exactly those that realise every existential demand they can express. The test is the standard tool for building elementary chains.
proof: Induct on formula complexity; atomic and boolean cases are immediate, and the existential direction is precisely the stated witness condition.
consequence: It is used in the downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem and in model-theoretic constructions.

title: Gödel's Completeness Theorem for First-Order Languages
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A first-order sentence is provable from a theory if and only if it is true in every model of that theory.
short: Syntactic provability and semantic truth coincide in first-order logic.
long: Syntactic provability and semantic truth coincide in first-order logic. This is distinct from Gödel's incompleteness theorems, which concern the limits of particular theories.
proof: Show that every consistent theory has a model by constructing a term model from maximal consistent sets (Henkin's proof), then apply contraposition.
consequence: It legitimises model-theoretic reasoning as a substitute for syntactic derivation.

title: The Compactness Theorem for First-Order Logic
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A set of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset has a model.
short: Finite consistency is enough to guarantee an infinite model.
long: Finite consistency is enough to guarantee an infinite model. It yields nonstandard models of arithmetic and the existence of infinite models from arbitrarily large finite ones.
proof: Combine completeness with the observation that if the whole set were inconsistent, a finite subset would already be inconsistent because formal proofs are finite.
consequence: It is one of the most powerful tools in model theory.

title: The Löwenheim–Skolem Theorems
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If a first-order theory in a countable language has an infinite model, it has models of every infinite cardinality at least the size of the language.
short: First-order theories cannot control the infinite size of their models.
long: First-order theories cannot control the infinite size of their models. Skolem's paradox is that set theory has countable models even though it proves uncountable sets exist.
proof: Use the downward theorem with elementary substructures generated by a chosen subset and the upward theorem by adding fresh constants and applying compactness.
consequence: It limits the expressive power of first-order logic and is central to model theory.

title: The Deduction Theorem
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A theory proves an implication from premise to conclusion exactly when extending the theory by that premise proves the conclusion.
short: Conditional proofs correspond to proving the consequent with the antecedent assumed.
long: Conditional proofs correspond to proving the consequent with the antecedent assumed. It holds for standard Hilbert-style and natural deduction systems for first-order logic.
proof: The forward direction uses modus ponens; the converse transforms any proof from the extended theory into a proof of the implication by induction on proof length.
consequence: It is the formal justification for the everyday method of conditional proof.
